newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major says EMU unlikely to start on time.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major says EMU unlikely to start on time.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major told parliament on Thursday he did not believe Europe's single currency would start on time in January 1999.

In his toughest warning that he is considering keeping Britain out of monetary union, he said there was no chance sterling would join a single currency if other European Union members "fudged" the economic entry criteria.

"It is very unlikely, though not impossible, that the single currency itself could proceed safely on January 1, 1999," Major told parliament. "But if it did proceed without reliable convergence we would not, of course, be part of it."
His statement came after a cabinet meeting to discuss Britain's approach to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the main aspect of which is the single currency.
Major's cabinet is split between ministers who want to rule out entry into a single currency during the next parliament and those who want to stick to the policy of keeping Britain's options open.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, cabinet's most pro-European member, told reporters as he left Major's office: "It is unlikely in my opinion we would start EMU on January 1. It's not impossible but it's unlikely that they will...
"We were proceeding on the basis of the policy that we're going to negotiate and decide at the right time, and that was accepted by everybody."

Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind added: "As the Chancellor pointed out and as the cabinet concluded, it is unlikely that circumstances would lead to us wishing to join a single currency in January 1999. The crucial requirement is always the national interest."
The cabinet had debated a Treasury report on whether other EU states were fulfilling the tough economic targets laid down for joining a single currency.
The paper was commissioned after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke came under pressure in December from members of the cabinet opposed to closer European integration.
Major has said a referendum will take place if the cabinet should ever decide to join the currency. But he had stopped short of ruling out entry.
Newspapers had billed Thursday's cabinet discussion as the last chance for Eurosceptics to get Major to change his mind.

Clarke has fought a bitter defence of the wait-and-see policy, which would allow Britain to decide whether or not to join the single currency when it goes ahead, even threatening to resign if Major bowed to the demands of the Eurosceptics.
Rifkind made it clear this week he believed neither the national nor the Conservative party's interests would be served by ditching the currency opt-out Major negotiated in 1991.
